claim: SARM1 regulates axonal degeneration through its NAD-metabolizing activity.
source: SARM1 regulates axonal degeneration through its NAD-metabolizing activity and is a drug target for neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about SARM1's mechanism of action.

claim: SARM1 is a drug target for neurodegenerative disorders.
source: SARM1 regulates axonal degeneration through its NAD-metabolizing activity and is a drug target for neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known therapeutic target.

claim: Fluorescent conjugates of styryl derivative with pyridine serve as substrates of SARM1.
source: We designed and synthesized fluorescent conjugates of styryl derivative with pyridine to serve as substrates of SARM1, which exhibited large red shifts after conversion.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing the probes function as SARM1 substrates.

claim: The fluorescent conjugates exhibited large red shifts after conversion by SARM1.
source: We designed and synthesized fluorescent conjugates of styryl derivative with pyridine to serve as substrates of SARM1, which exhibited large red shifts after conversion.
evidence: This is supported by spectroscopic data showing emission maximum shifts from 430 nm to 520 nm for PC6.

claim: SARM1 activation was visualized in live cells following elevation of endogenous NMN.
source: With the conjugates, SARM1 activation was visualized in live cells following elevation of endogenous NMN or treatment with a cell-permeant NMN-analog.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal imaging experiments showing PAD6 fluorescence in NMNAT1-KO cells.

claim: SARM1 activation was visualized in live cells following treatment with a cell-permeant NMN-analog.
source: With the conjugates, SARM1 activation was visualized in live cells following elevation of endogenous NMN or treatment with a cell-permeant NMN-analog.
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal imaging showing increased PAD6 fluorescence after CZ-48 treatment.

claim: Mouse SARM1 activation preceded vincristine-induced axonal degeneration by hours in neurons.
source: In neurons, imaging documented mouse SARM1 activation preceded vincristine-induced axonal degeneration by hours.
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data showing PAD6 fluorescence increase at 4-8 hours while axon degeneration started at about 20 hours.

claim: A derivative of nisoldipine (NSDP) is a covalent inhibitor of SARM1.
source: Library screening identified a derivative of nisoldipine (NSDP) as a covalent inhibitor of SARM1 that reacted with the cysteines, especially Cys311 in its ARM domain and blocked its NMN-activation, protecting axons from degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by screening data, irreversibility experiments, and LC-MS/MS identification of cysteine modifications.

claim: The nisoldipine derivative reacted with cysteines in SARM1, especially Cys311 in its ARM domain.
source: Library screening identified a derivative of nisoldipine (NSDP) as a covalent inhibitor of SARM1 that reacted with the cysteines, especially Cys311 in its ARM domain and blocked its NMN-activation, protecting axons from degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data showing Cys311 as the dominant modification site and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The nisoldipine derivative blocked SARM1 NMN-activation.
source: Library screening identified a derivative of nisoldipine (NSDP) as a covalent inhibitor of SARM1 that reacted with the cysteines, especially Cys311 in its ARM domain and blocked its NMN-activation, protecting axons from degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro and cellular assays showing inhibition of SARM1-dN but not SAM-TIR.

claim: The nisoldipine derivative protected axons from degeneration.
source: Library screening identified a derivative of nisoldipine (NSDP) as a covalent inhibitor of SARM1 that reacted with the cysteines, especially Cys311 in its ARM domain and blocked its NMN-activation, protecting axons from degeneration.
evidence: This is supported by DRG neuron experiments showing reduced axon degeneration after vincristine treatment and axotomy.

claim: The Cryo-EM structure showed that SARM1 was locked into an inactive conformation by the inhibitor.
source: The Cryo-EM structure showed that SARM1 was locked into an inactive conformation by the inhibitor, uncovering a potential neuroprotective mechanism of dihydropyridines.
evidence: This is supported by the 2.4 Å resolution cryo-EM structure showing structural similarity to NAD-bound SARM1.

claim: The inhibitor mechanism uncovers a potential neuroprotective mechanism of dihydropyridines.
source: The Cryo-EM structure showed that SARM1 was locked into an inactive conformation by the inhibitor, uncovering a potential neuroprotective mechanism of dihydropyridines.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and functional data showing dHNN (a dihydropyridine derivative) inhibits SARM1 and protects axons.

claim: Axon degeneration occurs in most neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Axon degeneration (AxD) occurs in most neurodegenerative disorders (Coleman and Höke, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Coleman and Höke, 2020.

claim: SARM1 acts as a main effector in axon degeneration.
source: Sterile Alpha and TIR Motif–containing 1 (SARM1) acts as a main effector in this process (Osterloh et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Osterloh et al., 2012.

claim: Depletion of SARM1 significantly attenuates axon degeneration.
source: and its depletion significantly attenuates AxD (Geisler et al., 2016; Osterloh et al., 2012; Turkiew et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: SARM1 controls axon degeneration through its enzymatic activity.
source: SARM1 controls AxD through its enzymatic activity (Essuman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Essuman et al., 2017.

claim: SARM1 is self-inhibitory and is activated by nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
source: It is self-inhibitory and is activated by nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Zhao et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: SARM1 activation results in depletion of the intracellular NAD-pool.
source: It is self-inhibitory and is activated by nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) (Zhao et al., 2019), resulting in depletion of the intracellular NAD-pool (Essuman et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Essuman et al., 2017 and Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: NAD itself is an inhibitor of SARM1 activation.
source: However, recent studies suggest that nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) itself is an inhibitor of SARM1 activation and the balance between NMN and NAD controls the activation of SARM1 (Figley et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The balance between NMN and NAD controls the activation of SARM1.
source: However, recent studies suggest that nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) itself is an inhibitor of SARM1 activation and the balance between NMN and NAD controls the activation of SARM1 (Figley et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: SARM1 is a multifunctional enzyme with properties similar to CD38.
source: We have documented that SARM1 is a multifunctional enzyme with properties similar to CD38, a universal signaling enzyme possessing not only NADase activity but also catalyzing both the cyclization of NAD to cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR) and the exchange of nicotinamide in NADP with nicotinic acid to produce nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: CD38 possesses NADase activity and catalyzes cyclization of NAD to cADPR.
source: We have documented that SARM1 is a multifunctional enzyme with properties similar to CD38, a universal signaling enzyme possessing not only NADase activity but also catalyzing both the cyclization of NAD to cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR) and the exchange of nicotinamide in NADP with nicotinic acid to produce nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD38 cited from Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: CD38 catalyzes the exchange of nicotinamide in NADP with nicotinic acid to produce NAADP.
source: We have documented that SARM1 is a multifunctional enzyme with properties similar to CD38, a universal signaling enzyme possessing not only NADase activity but also catalyzing both the cyclization of NAD to cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR) and the exchange of nicotinamide in NADP with nicotinic acid to produce nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NAADP) (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CD38 cited from Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: cADPR and NAADP are messengers regulating calcium mobilization.
source: Both cADPR and NAADP are messengers regulating calcium mobilization in the endoplasmic reticulum and the endo-lysosomes, respectively (reviewed in Galione, 1994; Lee, 2012; Lee and Zhao, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: cADPR regulates calcium mobilization in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Both cADPR and NAADP are messengers regulating calcium mobilization in the endoplasmic reticulum and the endo-lysosomes, respectively (reviewed in Galione, 1994; Lee, 2012; Lee and Zhao, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: NAADP regulates calcium mobilization in the endo-lysosomes.
source: Both cADPR and NAADP are messengers regulating calcium mobilization in the endoplasmic reticulum and the endo-lysosomes, respectively (reviewed in Galione, 1994; Lee, 2012; Lee and Zhao, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: SARM1 may be a calcium signaling enzyme.
source: The catalytic similarities and its ubiquitous presence in non-neuronal cells suggest that SARM1 may be a calcium signaling enzyme as well.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on similarities to CD38 and SARM1's distribution.

claim: Pyridyl derivatives can readily serve as substrates for SARM1's base-exchange reaction.
source: We focused on its base-exchange reaction for designing specific probes for SARM1 and had shown that pyridyl derivatives can readily serve as substrates (Graeff et al., 2006; Lee and Aarhus, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PC1-9 were synthesized using Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling strategy with yields ranging from 33.5 to 85.0%.
source: Pyridine conjugates (PC1-9, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 11A) were synthesized using the Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling strategy with yields ranging from 33.5 to 85.0%.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the synthesis method and yields.

claim: Significant shifts in UV-vis spectra were observed in reactions with oxygenated derivatives (PC5-8) but not nitrogenated derivatives (PC1-4) or PC9.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 12, significant shifts in UV-vis spectra were observed in the reactions with the oxygenated derivatives (PC5-8, O-series), but not the nitrogenated derivatives (PC1–4, N-series), nor PC9 with diene as linker.
evidence: This is supported by spectroscopic data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 12.

claim: PC6 exhibited the largest fluorescence increase among the reactive O-series probes.
source: The emission spectra of the reactive O-series showed steady increase as the reaction progressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 13, spectra; Figure 1D, kinetics; Figure 1—figure supplement 11C, initial rate), with PC6, the chemical structure shown in Figure 1C, exhibiting the largest fluorescence increase (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PC6 has an isosbestic point at 350 nm during the SARM1-catalyzed reaction.
source: The time course study for the reaction involving PC6 showed that the UV absorption decreases at 330 nm but increases at 400 nm with an isosbestic point at 350 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 12; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by spectroscopic data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PC6 has an emission maximum at 430 nm and PAD6 has an emission maximum at 520 nm.
source: Corresponding to the absorbance change was the red shift in the fluorescence spectra, from the emission maximum at 430 nm of PC6 to 520 nm of PAD6 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence spectroscopy data shown in Figure 1E and 1G.

claim: The conversion of PC6 to PAD6 was verified by HPLC and HRMS.
source: The conversion of PC6 to the exchange product, PAD6, was verified by purifying it using HPLC and characterized by high resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC and MS data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The emission maximum shift of over 100 nm is due to the pyridine ring becoming positively charged after exchange into NAD.
source: The remarkably large spectral changes are anticipated from our design, as the pyridine ring becomes positively charged after its exchange into NAD (Figure 1F, inlet), a much stronger electron acceptor in the D−π−A structure, thereby increasing intramolecular charge transfer and shifting the emission maximum by over 100 nm.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation based on the molecular design and observed spectral data.

claim: The spectral changes showed a linear dependence on NMN with as low as 10 μM being effective.
source: The observed spectral changes showed a linear dependence on NMN, with as low as 10 μM being effective (Figure 1H)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: SARM1 is an auto-inhibitory enzyme activated by NMN.
source: The observed spectral changes showed a linear dependence on NMN, with as low as 10 μM being effective (Figure 1H), confirming that SARM1 is an auto-inhibitory enzyme activated by NMN (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is confirmed by the NMN dose-dependence data and supported by citation.

claim: The fluorescence increase was proportional to the amount of NMN-activated SARM1.
source: The fluorescence increase was also proportional to the amount of NMN-activated SARM1 (Figure 1I)
evidence: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: PC6 has a detection limit of 48 ng/mL for SARM1.
source: The fluorescence increase was also proportional to the amount of NMN-activated SARM1 (Figure 1I), with a detection limit of 48 ng/mL.
evidence: This is calculated from the dose-response data.

claim: PC6 provides more than 100-fold higher sensitivity over εNAD, NGD, or NHD as an in vitro assay for SARM1.
source: As an in vitro assay for SARM1, PC6 provides more than 100-fold higher sensitivity over other commonly used probes, such as εNAD, NGD, or NHD (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by comparative assay data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: PC6 shows exquisite selectivity toward SARM1 versus CD38 and N. crassa NADase.
source: In addition to sensitivity, PC6 also shows exquisite selectivity toward SARM1 versus CD38 and N. crassa NADase (Graeff et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by comparative enzyme assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: SARM1, CD38, and N. crassa NADase all possess NADase activity as detected by εNAD.
source: All three possess NADase activity as detected by εNAD (Figure 1K), but only SARM1 could produce large fluorescence increase with PC6.
evidence: This is supported by comparative assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Only SARM1 could produce large fluorescence increase with PC6, not CD38 or N. crassa NADase.
source: All three possess NADase activity as detected by εNAD (Figure 1K), but only SARM1 could produce large fluorescence increase with PC6.
evidence: This is supported by comparative assay data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: Green fluorescence was clearly seen evenly distributed in whole cells overexpressing wildtype SARM1 but not in E642A mutant cells after PC6 treatment.
source: PC6 was added to HEK293 cells overexpressing either wildtype SARM1 or the enzymatically inactive mutant, E642A (Essuman et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2019; Figure 2A). Green fluorescence was clearly seen evenly distributed in the whole cells in the wildtype, but not in the mutant cells (Figure 2B), indicating active SARM1 was required.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Active SARM1 is required for PAD6 production in cells.
source: Green fluorescence was clearly seen evenly distributed in the whole cells in the wildtype, but not in the mutant cells (Figure 2B), indicating active SARM1 was required.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison between wildtype and E642A mutant cells.

claim: Intracellular production of PAD6 was confirmed in extracts of wildtype but not E642A cells.
source: Intracellular production of PAD6 was confirmed in extracts of wildtype but not the E642A cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC and MS analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CZ-48 dramatically increased PAD6 fluorescence in wildtype SARM1-expressing cells but not in E642A cells.
source: CZ-48, a cell-permeant mimetic of NMN and activator of SARM1 (Zhao et al., 2019), dramatically increased the PAD6 fluorescence (Figure 2B, right column) and none in E642A-cells.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PC6 is cell-permeant.
source: These results indicate that PC6 is cell-permeant and can be exchanged into the cytosolic NAD by the activated SARM1 to produce PAD6 having a large red shift in fluorescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of intracellular PAD6 production after PC6 treatment.

claim: PAD6 is cell-impermeant and accumulates in the cytosol.
source: PAD6 was also cell-impermeant because of its charged ADP-ribose moiety and accumulated in the cytosol, greatly increased its detection sensitivity in live cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular structure of PAD6 containing a charged ADP-ribose moiety.

claim: PC6 can detect the activity of endogenously expressed SARM1 in HEK293T cells.
source: PC6 also could detect the activity of SARM1 endogenously expressed in HEK293T cells (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data showing PAD6 fluorescence in wildtype but not SARM1-KO cells after CZ-48 treatment.

claim: CZ-48 activated endogenous SARM1 and produced increase of cytosolic PAD6 signal in HEK293T cells.
source: CZ-48 activated the endogenous SARM1 and produced increase of cytosolic PAD6 signal (Figure 2D, upper right), but none in the SARM1-knockout cells (Figure 2D, right lower), confirming the specificity of PC6 for SARM1.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: No PAD6 signal was detected in SARM1-knockout cells after CZ-48 treatment, confirming the specificity of PC6 for SARM1.
source: CZ-48 activated the endogenous SARM1 and produced increase of cytosolic PAD6 signal (Figure 2D, upper right), but none in the SARM1-knockout cells (Figure 2D, right lower), confirming the specificity of PC6 for SARM1.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data comparing wildtype and SARM1-KO cells in Figure 2D.

claim: Without Dox induction, only basal SARM1 with minimal activity was detected in the inducible cell line.
source: Without induction, only basal SARM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) with minimal activity was detected (Figure 2E, green dots)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E and Western blot in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CZ-48 activation of basal SARM1 resulted in increase in PAD6-fluorescence.
source: Without induction, only basal SARM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) with minimal activity was detected (Figure 2E, green dots), while activated by CZ-48, resulting in increase in PAD6-fluorescence (orange triangles).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Induction of SARM1 by Dox produced minimal PAD6 signal, confirming SARM1 is auto-inhibitory.
source: Induction of SARM1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) produced minimal signal also (Figure 2E, purple squares), confirming SARM1 is auto-inhibitory.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Both basal and induced SARM1 were activated by CZ-48, resulting in the largest PAD6 signal.
source: With CZ-48, both the basal and the induced SARM1 were activated, resulting in the largest signal (Figure 2E, black triangles).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: No PAD6 signal was detected in SARM1-knockout cells in the inducible system.
source: In SARM1-knockout cells, no signal was detected (Figure 2D, SARM1-KO; Figure 2E, blue and red dots).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Endogenous NMN can be increased by ablating NMNAT1 to activate SARM1.
source: Endogenous NMN can be increased by ablating NMN-adenylytransferase (NMNAT1) (Zhao et al., 2019) to activate SARM1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019.

claim: NMNAT1 knockout in HEK293T cells resulted in increasing PAD6 fluorescence in a time-dependent manner.
source: Correspondingly, NMNAT1 knockout in HEK293T cells also resulted in increasing PAD6 fluorescence (Figure 2F) in a time-dependent manner (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 2F and 2G.

claim: PC6 is highly selective for SARM1 over CD38 in live cells.
source: Consistent with the in vitro results showing that PC6 is highly selective for SARM1 over CD38 in live cells, cells expressing either wildtype or Type III mutant CD38 (Liu et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2012) did not show PAD6-signal after 48 hr incubation with PC6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Cells expressing wildtype or Type III mutant CD38 did not show PAD6-signal after 48 hr incubation with PC6.
source: Consistent with the in vitro results showing that PC6 is highly selective for SARM1 over CD38 in live cells, cells expressing either wildtype or Type III mutant CD38 (Liu et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2012) did not show PAD6-signal after 48 hr incubation with PC6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expressed CD38 enzymes readily increased cellular cADPR.
source: Consistent with the in vitro results showing that PC6 is highly selective for SARM1 over CD38 in live cells, cells expressing either wildtype or Type III mutant CD38 (Liu et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2012) did not show PAD6-signal after 48 hr incubation with PC6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), even though the expressed enzymes readily increased cellular cADPR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cADPR measurement data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vincristine-induced axon degeneration in peripheral neuropathy is a common side effect of chemotherapy.
source: Vincristine (VCR)-induced AxD in peripheral neuropathy is a common side effect of chemotherapy (Essuman et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Essuman et al., 2017.

claim: Vincristine-induced axon degeneration is thought to be due to SARM1-activation.
source: Vincristine (VCR)-induced AxD in peripheral neuropathy is a common side effect of chemotherapy (Essuman et al., 2017) and is thought to be due to SARM1-activation (Gerdts et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerdts et al., 2013.

claim: VCR elevated PAD6-fluorescence in DRG neurons with non-targeting shRNA by as early as 4-8 hr, reaching maximum by 16 hr.
source: In the non-targeting group, VCR elevated PAD6-fluorescence (Figure 3A, green), indicating activation of SARM1, by as early as 4–8 hr and reaching a maximum by 16 hr (Figure 3A and D, blue).
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: Axon degeneration started at about 20 hr after VCR treatment in DRG neurons.
source: AxD started at about 20 hr (Figure 3F, blue; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by axon degeneration index data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The timing of SARM1 activation is temporally consistent with a causal role for SARM1 in axon degeneration.
source: AxD started at about 20 hr (Figure 3F, blue; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), temporally consistent with a causal role for SARM1.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between SARM1 activation (4-16 hr) and axon degeneration (starting at 20 hr).

claim: Cellular cADPR elevation occurred by 12 hr after VCR treatment, peaking at 24 hr.
source: Another measure of SARM1 activation is the elevation of cellular cADPR (Zhao et al., 2019), which occurred (Figure 3E, blue) by 12 hr, peaking at 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by cADPR measurement data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Neurons not treated with VCR showed neither SARM1-activation nor axon degeneration.
source: Neurons not treated with VCR showed neither SARM1-activation nor AxD (Figure 3A,D,E,F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, CTRL).
evidence: This is supported by control data shown in Figures 3A, 3D, 3E, 3F.

claim: Reducing endogenous SARM1 using shRNA reduced PAD6 fluorescence without altering its peaking at 16 hr.
source: Reducing endogenous SARM1 using shRNA (Figure 3B,D and F, KD) reduced the PAD6 fluorescence without altering its peaking at 16 hr (Figure 3C; 3D, KD +VCR)
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: Reducing endogenous SARM1 using shRNA reduced axon degeneration.
source: Reducing endogenous SARM1 using shRNA (Figure 3B,D and F, KD) reduced the PAD6 fluorescence without altering its peaking at 16 hr (Figure 3C; 3D, KD +VCR) and reduced AxD (Figure 3F, KD +VCR; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by axon degeneration index data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The reduction in axon degeneration by SARM1 knockdown further substantiates a causal role for SARM1.
source: Reducing endogenous SARM1 using shRNA (Figure 3B,D and F, KD) reduced the PAD6 fluorescence without altering its peaking at 16 hr (Figure 3C; 3D, KD +VCR) and reduced AxD (Figure 3F, KD +VCR; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), further substantiating a causal role for SARM1.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic loss-of-function experiment showing reduced axon degeneration.

claim: CZ-48 induced SARM1-activation more rapidly than VCR.
source: CZ-48 induced SARM1-activation more rapidly (Figure 3A and D, red)
evidence: This is supported by time-course data shown in Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: CZ-48 elevated cADPR higher than VCR.
source: CZ-48 induced SARM1-activation more rapidly (Figure 3A and D, red) and elevated cADPR higher (Figure 3E, red)
evidence: This is supported by cADPR measurement data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CZ-48 confirms direct action on SARM1.
source: CZ-48 induced SARM1-activation more rapidly (Figure 3A and D, red) and elevated cADPR higher (Figure 3E, red), confirming its direct action.
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid and strong activation by CZ-48, a known SARM1 activator.

claim: CZ-48 did not induce massive axon degeneration as VCR did.
source: Intriguingly, CZ-48 did not induce massive AxD as VCR (Figure 3F, CZ-48; S5A).
evidence: This is supported by axon degeneration index data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SARM1-activation is a necessary and causal factor, but not a sufficient one for axon degeneration.
source: These results indicate SARM1-activation is a necessary and causal factor, but not a sufficient one for AxD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CZ-48 activates SARM1 but does not cause massive axon degeneration like VCR.

claim: Other critical factors and downstream events of microtubular dysfunction might contribute to axon degeneration.
source: Other critical factors and downstream events of microtubular dysfunction might contribute to the degeneration.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observation that SARM1 activation alone is not sufficient for axon degeneration.

claim: The measured IC50 value of nicotinamide for SARM1 inhibition was around 140 μM, consistent with reported values.
source: The feasibility was verified by measuring the IC50 of a reported inhibitor of SARM1, nicotinamide (Nam) (Essuman et al., 2017). The measured IC50 value of Nam was around 140 μM, which is consistent with the reported value (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citation to Essuman et al., 2017.

claim: Out of 2015 drugs screened, 34 had more than 80% inhibition of SARM1.
source: Out of 2015 drugs, 34 had more than 80% inhibition (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by high-throughput screening data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Twenty-four drugs inhibited both PC6 and NADase reactions similarly.
source: Twenty-four drugs are in the middle sector, indicating they inhibited both reactions similarly.
evidence: This is supported by the IC50 comparison plot shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Two drugs inhibited the PC6 activity five fold less than the NADase.
source: Two inhibited the PC6 activity five fold less than the NADase (Figure 4C, left sector)
evidence: This is supported by the IC50 comparison plot shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Eight drugs inhibited NADase less than the base-exchange reaction.
source: and eight in the right sector (seven have IC50s higher than 40 μM) inhibited NADase less than the base-exchange.
evidence: This is supported by the IC50 comparison plot shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The remarkable differences in inhibition between assays underscore the importance of using more than one assay for drug screening.
source: These remarkable differences underscore the importance of using more than one assay for drug screening (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of differential inhibition patterns between PC6 and NADase assays.

claim: Nisoldipine is a calcium channel blocker having beneficial effects on neurodegenerative diseases.
source: In the middle sector is nisoldipine (NSDP), a calcium channel blocker having beneficial effects on neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about nisoldipine.

claim: The inhibition of SARM1 by nisoldipine varied widely among batches.
source: Peculiarly, its inhibition of SARM1 varied widely among batches.
evidence: This is an observation from the screening experiments.

claim: The active compound inhibiting SARM1 was not nisoldipine but its derivative.
source: Investigations indicated the active compound was not NSDP but its derivative.
evidence: This is inferred from the UV treatment experiments showing increased potency.

claim: Fresh nisoldipine had an IC50 of about 150 μM for SARM1 inhibition.
source: Figure 4D shows fresh NSDP had an IC50-value of about 150 μM (squares)
evidence: This is supported by IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: UV exposure increased nisoldipine's potency 75-fold with IC50 = 2.36 ± 0.3 μM.
source: but its potency increased 75-fold after exposure to UV (Figure 4D, triangles, IC50 = 2.36 ± 0.3 μM).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fresh nisoldipine had an HPLC-elution peak at 12.2 min.
source: Also, fresh NSDP had an HPLC-elution peak at 12.2 min (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: UV treatment completely converted nisoldipine to a compound with HPLC peak at 9.8 min that strongly inhibited SARM1.
source: but was completely converted by UV to a compound having a peak at 9.8 min that strongly inhibited SARM1 (Figure 4E, red).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC and activity assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The active compound had a mass of 370.15205 Da, identical to dehydronitrosonisoldipine (dHNN).
source: HRMS showed that the active compound had a mass of 370.15205 Da (Figure 4E, inset) identical to a known derivative of NSDP, dehydronitrosonisoldipine (dHNN) (Marinkovic et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by HRMS data shown in Figure 4E and citation to Marinkovic et al., 2003.

claim: The HPLC-elution profile of the active compound was the same as authentic dHNN.
source: The HPLC-elution profile of the active compound was also the same as dHNN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, purple line and green dash).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC comparison data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Authentic dHNN was active and could not be further activated by UV.
source: Indeed, authentic dHNN was active and could not be further activated by UV (Figure 4F, red line and dash)
evidence: This is supported by IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: dHNN is photostable.
source: Indeed, authentic dHNN was active and could not be further activated by UV (Figure 4F, red line and dash), which also indicates that it is photostable.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UV treatment does not change dHNN's activity.

claim: Dehydronisoldipine (dHN) showed no inhibition before or after UV treatment.
source: Another derivative of NSDP, dehydronisoldipine (dHN, elution peak at 8.7 min, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), showed no inhibition before or after UV (Figure 4F, black line and dash)
evidence: This is supported by IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The nitroso group is essential for SARM1 inhibition by nisoldipine derivatives.
source: Another derivative of NSDP, dehydronisoldipine (dHN, elution peak at 8.7 min, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), showed no inhibition before or after UV (Figure 4F, black line and dash), indicating that the nitroso group is essential for the effect.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing dHNN (active, has nitroso group) with dHN (inactive, lacks nitroso group).

claim: dHNN-induced inhibition of SARM1 was irreversible by washing.
source: The dHNN-induced inhibition of SARM1 was irreversible by washing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, red bars), while that by Nam was reversible.
evidence: This is supported by washing experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Nicotinamide-induced inhibition of SARM1 was reversible by washing.
source: The dHNN-induced inhibition of SARM1 was irreversible by washing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, red bars), while that by Nam was reversible.
evidence: This is supported by washing experiment data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: dHNN-inhibition was time-dependent, but not nicotinamide inhibition.
source: Also, dHNN-inhibition was time-dependent, but not Nam (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is supported by time-course inhibition data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The irreversibility and time-dependence strongly suggest dHNN covalently reacted with SARM1.
source: Also, dHNN-inhibition was time-dependent, but not Nam (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), strongly suggesting dHNN covalently reacted with SARM1.
evidence: This is inferred from the irreversibility and time-dependence of inhibition, characteristic of covalent modification.

claim: SAM-TIR (ARM-domain truncated) showed a right-shifted inhibition curve compared to SARM1-dN with around 50-fold increase in IC50.
source: To determine the mechanism of action of dHNN, we truncated the inhibitory ARM-domain, producing a constitutively active SAM-TIR, which showed a right-shifted inhibition curve compared to SARM1-dN (Figure 5A), with around 50-fold increase in the IC50.
evidence: This is supported by IC50 comparison data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The IC50 of dHNN in SARM1-dN-expression cells is around 4 μM, close to the IC50 in vitro.
source: The IC50 of dHNN in the SARM1-dN-expression cells is around 4 μM, close to the IC50 in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by cellular assay data.

claim: dHNN decreased cellular cADPR in cells expressing SARM1, but not in those expressing SAM-TIR.
source: dHNN decreased the cellular cADPR in cells expressing SARM1, but not in those expressing SAM-TIR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by cADPR measurement data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: dHNN is cell-permeant and acts mainly by blocking SARM1 activation but not its enzymatic activities.
source: These results suggest that dHNN is cell-permeant and acts mainly by blocking SARM1 activation but not its enzymatic activities.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects on SARM1-dN versus SAM-TIR.

claim: LC-MS/MS identified Cys311 in the ARM domain as the dominant dHNN modification site.
source: The nitroso group of dHNN may covalently modify cysteine residues (Callan et al., 2009) in SARM1. Indeed, LC-MS/MS identified several dHNN-modified peptides, among which Cys311 in the ARM domain is the dominant one (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many peptides of other proteins with cysteines were identified but none showed modification by dHNN, indicating specificity.
source: Many peptides of other proteins with cysteines were also identified but none showed modification by dHNN (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating specificity of dHNN.
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: C311A mutation significantly decreased the response to dHNN.
source: Single mutation of all the cysteines to alanine showed that C311A significantly decreased the response to dHNN (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis and IC50 measurement data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The IC50 of C311A was only two fold higher than wildtype, suggesting dHNN might modify other cysteines when Cys311 is mutated.
source: However, the IC50 of C311A was only two fold higher than that of the wildtype, which indicates dHNN might modify other cysteines when Cys311 is mutated and inactivate SARM1.
evidence: This is inferred from the modest IC50 shift in the C311A mutant.

claim: dHNN stabilized a similar inhibitory conformation of SARM1 as that induced by NAD.
source: With Cryo-EM, we found that dHNN stabilized a similar inhibitory conformation of SARM1 as that induced by NAD (PDB: 7cm6) (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM structural data and comparison with NAD-bound structure.

claim: In 2D-classification of untreated SARM1, most particles presented only the SAM octamer ring.
source: In 2D-classification of the untreated SARM1, most particles presented only the SAM octamer ring (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D classification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A.

claim: For dHNN-treated SARM1, larger octamer ring corresponding to both SAM and ARM/TIR domains could be clearly observed.
source: For the dHNN-treated SARM1, larger octamer ring corresponding to both the SAM and ARM/TIR domains could be clearly observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM 2D classification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The 3D-structure of dHNN-treated SARM1 was constructed at 2.4 Å resolution.
source: Its 3D-structure was constructed at 2.4 Å resolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Residues from 56 to 549 (ARM and SAM domains) and 561 to 702 (TIR domain) were fitted into the cryo-EM map.
source: Its 3D-structure was constructed at 2.4 Å resolution (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C) with residues from 56 to 549 (ARM and SAM domains) and 561 to 702 (TIR domain) all fitted into the cryo-EM map (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Structural superimposition with NAD-bound SARM1 showed RMSD values of 0.91.
source: Structural superimposition with the NAD-bound SARM1 (PDB: 7cm6) (Jiang et al., 2020) showed RMSD values of 0.91 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E)
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3E.

claim: dHNN constrains SARM1 in an inactive conformation similar to that induced by NAD.
source: Structural superimposition with the NAD-bound SARM1 (PDB: 7cm6) (Jiang et al., 2020) showed RMSD values of 0.91 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E), suggesting that dHNN constrains SARM1 in an inactive conformation similar to that induced by NAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the low RMSD value indicating structural similarity.

claim: Extra electron density was only observed near residue Cys311 in the cryo-EM structure.
source: Extra electron density was only observed near residue Cys311, the dHNN-target (Figure 5C and D), but not other cysteine residues, consistent with it being derived from dHNN (5F, purple).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM density map shown in Figure 5F.

claim: dHNN interacts with Glu264, Leu268, Arg307, Phe308, and Ala315 in the ARM domain.
source: dHNN interacts with Glu264, Leu268, Arg307, Phe308, and Ala315 (Figure 5F and Figure 5G, green) in the ARM domain
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: dHNN pushes the insertion loop toward ARM1 and stabilizes the ARM domain.
source: dHNN interacts with Glu264, Leu268, Arg307, Phe308, and Ala315 (Figure 5F and Figure 5G, green) in the ARM domain, pushing the insertion loop (Figure 5F, red) toward ARM1 and stabilizes the domain.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: The dHNN mechanism is similar to NAD, which binds at the other side of the insertion loop and stabilizes the ARM domain.
source: This is similar to that observed with NAD, which binds at the other side of the insertion loop and stabilizes the ARM domain possibly via ligating ARM1 and the insertion loop (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison shown in Figure 5G.

claim: dHNN inhibited VCR-activated cADPR production in neurons.
source: By preventing SARM1 from activation, dHNN also inhibited the VCR-activated cADPR production (Figure 5H) in neurons
evidence: This is supported by cADPR measurement data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: dHNN blocked VCR-induced axon degeneration as effectively as knocking out SARM1.
source: By preventing SARM1 from activation, dHNN also inhibited the VCR-activated cADPR production (Figure 5H) in neurons and blocked not only the VCR-induced AxD (Figure 5I, third picture; Figure 5J, red line), as effective as knocking out SARM1 (Figure 5I, fourth picture)
evidence: This is supported by axon degeneration data shown in Figures 5I and 5J.

claim: dHNN blocked axon degeneration after axotomy.
source: By preventing SARM1 from activation, dHNN also inhibited the VCR-activated cADPR production (Figure 5H) in neurons and blocked not only the VCR-induced AxD (Figure 5I, third picture; Figure 5J, red line), as effective as knocking out SARM1 (Figure 5I, fourth picture), but also AxD after axotomy (Figure 5—figure supplement 4A, third column; B, red line).
evidence: This is supported by axotomy experiment data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: PC probes are particularly advantageous because they are cell-permeant while the products are not and accumulate in the cytosol.
source: The PC probes developed here are particularly advantageous. They are cell-permeant, but the SARM1-catalyzed exchange products are not and accumulate in the cytosol, enhancing their detection.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular properties and observed cellular distribution.

claim: The large red shift of the product fluorescence provides easy visualization away from autofluorescence interference.
source: The remarkably large red shift of the product fluorescence provides easy visualization away from the interference of autofluorescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the spectral properties showing >100 nm red shift.

claim: Current fluorescent probes for SARM1 activity are all analogs of NAD and are cell-impermeant.
source: Currently, there are several fluorescent probes for SARM1 activity in use. They are all analogs of NAD and are cell-impermeant, such as εNAD.
evidence: This is stated as known information about existing probes.

claim: NAD analog probes may affect SARM1 activity since NAD is an inhibitor of SARM1.
source: The fact that NAD is now shown to be an inhibitor of SARM1 (Jiang et al., 2020; Sporny et al., 2020) makes the use of these analog probes problematic, as they may affect SARM1 activity as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the known inhibitory effect of NAD on SARM1.

claim: PC6 has no drawback of affecting SARM1 activity as it is a pyridine, not an NAD analog.
source: PC6 has no such drawback as it is a pyridine, not an NAD analog.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular structure of PC6.

claim: The use of PC6 requires neither expression of construct nor cell manipulation.
source: Furthermore, the use of PC6 requires neither expression of construct nor cell manipulation, making it suitable for detecting SARM1 activity in any cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the various cell types tested in the study.

claim: This study provided the first direct evidence in live DRG neurons that SARM1 activation precedes axon degeneration by several hours.
source: With the probes, we provided the first direct evidence in live DRG neurons that SARM1 activation precedes AxD by several hours
evidence: This is supported by time-course imaging data in DRG neurons.

claim: SARM1 is a necessary but insufficient factor for axon degeneration.
source: With the probes, we provided the first direct evidence in live DRG neurons that SARM1 activation precedes AxD by several hours and that it is a necessary but insufficient factor for AxD.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CZ-48 activates SARM1 but does not cause massive axon degeneration.

claim: Compounds may target the regulatory ARM domain or the catalytic TIR domain of SARM1.
source: The case for SARM1 is more complicated, as it is not only a multi-domain protein but also an auto-regulated enzyme catalyzing multiple reactions. Compounds may target the regulatory ARM domain as shown here for dHNN, or the catalytic TIR domain as Nam and the inhibitors reported during the preparation of this manuscript (Hughes et al., 2021; Loring et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the structural and functional data for dHNN and citations to other inhibitors.

claim: The substrates are different for the base-exchange and NADase reactions and may be differentially affected by inhibitor-induced conformational changes.
source: For SARM1, the substrates are different for the base-exchange and the NADase reactions and may thus be differentially affected by the inhibitor-induced conformational changes of the catalytic site.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed differential inhibition patterns.

claim: Many believe that the NADase activity of SARM1 is its dominant property for regulating axon degeneration.
source: Many believe that the NADase activity of SARM1, leading to cellular NAD depletion, is its dominant property for regulating AxD.
evidence: This is stated as a common belief in the field.

claim: The calcium messengers cADPR and NAADP produced by SARM1 may have functional roles in axon degeneration.
source: But the two calcium messengers, cADPR and NAADP produced by its cyclizing and base-exchange reactions may well have functional roles as well.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about potential roles of SARM1's other enzymatic products.

claim: Compounds with differential inhibition can be an important tool to resolve the functional roles of SARM1's different activities.
source: Compounds with differential inhibition can thus be an important tool to resolve the issue.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of differential inhibition patterns.

claim: dHNN is the first compound ever described that can block the activation of SARM1.
source: dHNN uncovered in this study is the first compound ever described that can block the activation of SARM1, revealing a druggable allosteric site
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: dHNN reveals a druggable allosteric site in SARM1.
source: dHNN uncovered in this study is the first compound ever described that can block the activation of SARM1, revealing a druggable allosteric site
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing dHNN binding to the ARM domain.

claim: dHNN can usher in a new approach for therapeutic drug development targeting SARM1.
source: dHNN uncovered in this study is the first compound ever described that can block the activation of SARM1, revealing a druggable allosteric site and can thus usher in a new approach for therapeutic drug development.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about the therapeutic potential of the findings.

claim: Metabolic conversion of nisoldipine to dHNN may account for the neural protective effects of nisoldipine.
source: Another point of interest is that dHNN is a derivative of NSDP. Metabolic conversion of NSDP to dHNN, leading to inhibition of SARM1, may well account for the neural protective effects of NSDP (Siddiqi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the finding that dHNN is a nisoldipine derivative and citation to neuroprotective effects.
